title: Tell me about a time you took ownership beyond your role
prompt: Tell me about a time you noticed a problem with unclear ownership and helped make sure it was addressed. Explain what you did within your responsibility, who else needed to be involved and what happened. Taking appropriate action can include a careful handoff or escalation.
blurb: Ownership: did the candidate act like the problem was theirs — end to end — or wait for someone else to own it?

rubric.label: Situation & stakes
rubric.description: Explains a specific problem, why it mattered and what was unclear about responsibility.

rubric.label: Why they owned it
rubric.description: Explains why they acted and the limits of their responsibility, including arranging an appropriate owner rather than personally doing every task.

rubric.label: Specific contribution and decisions
rubric.description: Describes a concrete contribution such as checking facts, notifying the responsible person, coordinating or following up; no particular pronouns are required.

rubric.label: Outcome and evidence
rubric.description: Describes a supported qualitative or quantitative outcome and how their action contributed, including an unresolved issue or a completed handoff.

rubric.label: Reflection & judgment
rubric.description: Explains the boundary between helpful initiative and overstepping and what would make ownership or follow-through clearer next time.

rubric.label: Clear, relevant communication
rubric.description: Makes the relevant situation, reasoning and contribution understandable in any clear order. No required STAR structure, pronouns, performance of confidence or emotional tone.

reference.scenario: Explore accountability for a problem that might otherwise be missed. The candidate can demonstrate ownership by acting within scope, finding the right owner, escalating or following through on a handoff. Assess responsible contribution rather than unsupervised work outside their authority.
model_points: Describes the problem and why the existing ownership or handoff was unclear.
Identifies their role and the authority or expertise needed to address it.
Takes a concrete safe step or communicates the issue to an appropriate person.
Checks the handoff or next step within what was reasonably available to them.
Describes what changed and distinguishes their contribution from others’ work.
Reflects on a useful prevention, ownership clarification or follow-up practice.

probes.trigger: candidate claims full ownership without stating their role
probes.question: What was within your responsibility here?

probes.trigger: candidate mentions a handoff but no next step
probes.question: How did you check that the concern reached the right person?
What did you observe after your action?

red_flags: Acts outside required authorization despite recognizing the boundary.
Conceals an unresolved risk while claiming it has been handled.
Takes credit for an outcome their own account attributes to someone else.
follow_ups: What made a handoff or escalation appropriate?
What would make responsibility clearer in a similar situation?
reference.exemplar_answer: Illustrative example only; it is not a required setting, answer order or achievement standard. At the start of a shift I noticed a damaged cable near a shared workstation. I did not try to repair it. I kept people away in line with our procedure, told the supervisor where it was and checked that the workstation was taken out of use. A qualified person later replaced it. My contribution was recognizing the issue and making a clear handoff, not performing the repair.
reference.assessment_contract: Assess the selected competency from concrete job-relevant evidence. Examples from paid work, study, volunteering, caregiving, informal work, military service and community activities are equally eligible when relevant. A modest example is sufficient if it shows the competency; employer prestige, formal title and financial scale are not criteria. Accept qualitative or quantitative outcomes supported by the account, including partial or unsuccessful outcomes. Do not require a numeric metric, STAR order, particular pronouns, composure, enthusiasm or a particular communication style. Identify personal contribution by meaning while preserving credit to others. Assess intelligibility and relevance, not accent, fluency, verbosity, visible emotion, disability or private circumstances. Mark genuinely missing evidence not assessed; do not infer poor competence or dishonesty from an absent example. A clearly labeled hypothetical may be discussed as situational practice but must not count as demonstrated past experience. Respect scope of practice, authorization, safety and ethical duties; pausing, declining, reporting or escalating can be sound judgment. Never require obedience, direct confrontation, unpaid overwork or successful persuasion regardless of the circumstances.
